events.title: Telegram
events.text:
RIYADH AIRPORT: Terminal 4 struck for the 2nd time in 24 hours. What we know so far.
Saturday, October 10:
A missile struck the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport, affecting Terminals 3 and 4 and triggering a mass evacuation.
Saudi aviation officials reported at least 12 killed and 309 wounded, including several in serious condition.
The dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and citizens of the U.S., Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan.
Witnesses described a projectile approaching the airport before an explosion caused part of the ceiling near a departure gate to collapse.
Sunday, October 11:
Saudi coalition spokesman Turki al Malki said another projectile struck Terminal 4, igniting a fire.
The extent of the damage remains unclear. No additional casualty figures have been released.
Separately, the coalition reported intercepting a ballistic missile over Al Kharj, near Prince Sultan Air Base, while another projectile reportedly landed near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
The wider picture:
Attacks on Riyadh airport between October 8 and 10 killed at least 15 people and wounded more than 300.
On October 8, 3 Saudis were killed in strikes targeting airport facilities and a Saudia aircraft. The Houthis claimed to have launched 2 cruise missiles at the airport.
The Saudi coalition has described the attacks as a war crime and threatened a decisive response.
President Donald Trump condemned the strikes and said he was considering U.S. participation in Saudi military operations against the Houthis.
What remains unknown:
Saudi authorities have not identified the weapon used in Sunday’s strike, confirmed whether Terminal 4 was occupied at the time, or released a new casualty assessment.
The latest strike comes as Riyadh hosts the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together senior oil ministers and energy executives.
The airport is a civilian aviation facility, and no military installation has been identified within the terminal complex.

🇾🇪⚔️ Houthis become one of the Middle East's most powerful armed forces
Yemen's Houthis have evolved from an insurgency into one of the Middle East's most powerful non-state military forces, according to the Financial Times. Their growing capabilities were demonstrated by three strikes on Riyadh's international airport within a week, one of which reportedly killed 12 people and injured more than 300.
The newspaper cites military and regional experts who identify several factors behind the Houthis' expanding power:
🟥 Advanced missile arsenal: The Houthis operate Palestine-2 ballistic missiles, long-range Asef anti-ship missiles, Quds cruise missiles, and Iranian-designed Type 358 anti-aircraft weapons, alongside explosive drone boats.
🟥 Domestic weapons production: The Houthis can now manufacture Samad attack drones largely independently, using locally produced fiberglass and commercially available components.
🟥 Surviving Western airstrikes: Years of US, UK, and Israeli bombardment have failed to eliminate their missile capabilities. In May 2025, a Houthi missile struck near Ben Gurion Airport despite the Pentagon reporting attacks on 1,000 targets in Yemen since March.
🟥 Improved battlefield coordination: Intelligence gathering, communications hacking, and coordinated operations helped the Houthis capture the strategic port of Mocha. Analysts also highlight their better-trained commanders and organizational cohesion.
🟥 Control over strategic waterways: The capture of Perim Island near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait has strengthened the Houthis' ability to threaten commercial shipping, particularly with explosive drone boats.
🟥 Expanding technological capabilities: An Anthropic security report identified attempts by users in Houthi-controlled Yemen to employ AI in missile development.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping, with the FT reporting that their blockade of Saudi ports has severely disrupted oil exports.

The escalating Houthi campaign is inflicting deep economic damage on Saudi Arabia, jeopardizing Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's plans to transform the oil-dependent economy, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Even the AI hub push now carries new risks, with data centers emerging as targets.

events.text:
🤔 Why the US isn’t strong enough to make Iran’s economy collapse
 
Treasury chief [Scott Bessent](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75438) predicted in late September that Iran’s economy would collapse within two weeks after its remaining oil shipments to China arrived and the ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ campaign to choke Tehran off from every single source of income and resources shifted into high gear.
Two weeks on, Iran is still there, as resilient and stubbornly resistant to US pressure as ever despite more than a year of kinetic, economic and shadow wars by enemies. Here’s why:
➡️ Iran has decades of experience living under the toughest sanctions the US and the global institutions it controls can serve up, targeting everything from trade, shipping and sovereign assets to tech transfers, banking, agricultural inputs, medical equipment, civil aviation, and consumer goods.
➡️ The country has a massive, [highly diversified industrial base](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/50976) and associated export portfolio, from steel and petrochemicals to cars, industrial machinery, complex turbines, food, and even high tech like nano, polymers and pharma.
➡️ Non-oil exports account for up to 45% of Iran’s foreign trade (in Saudi Arabia it’s 28%), and a diversified domestic economy means much of what Iran does import is not essential, and can be replaced using import-substitution, often at a lower cost.
➡️ Despite limited farmlands, difficult climatic conditions and limited rainfall, Iran [has created ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/70668)a world-class agricultural sector accounting for up to ~85% of its subsistence needs.
➡️ Iran is completely energy self-sufficient, and has proven itself capable to rapidly repairing damage to the sector after devastating US-Israeli attacks.
➡️ Together, the latter two factors mean the country can’t be starved or enervated into submission[ by Washington.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/64231)
Over a long enough timeframe, a sustained US campaign targeting Iran’s exports would have a major deleterious impact on the overall economy, but observers say the US is far more vulnerable to economic and energy warfare than Tehran in the short term, leaving it only a matter of time before [Washington is forced to fold](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75711?single), or collapse its own economy and the dollar system on which it’s based.
